title: From Beer to Paint to French Fries, the Iran War Is Hitting American Wallets
excerpt: The Strait of Hormuz closure is pushing up costs for raw materials and freight, forcing companies from Boston Beer to Sherwin-Williams to raise prices on everyday goods.
body:
• Boston Beer, Sherwin-Williams, International Paper, Unilever and Lamb Weston are among companies raising prices to offset Iran war-driven commodity costs.
  • Benchmark U.S. crude has risen about 25% to roughly $85 a barrel since the conflict began, with gasoline at $4.11 per gallon, up from $2.98.
  • Sherwin-Williams announced an 8% price increase effective September 1; its shares jumped more than 8% on the news.
  • The Fed voted 9-3 to hold rates unchanged, with Chairman Warsh flagging uncertainty over how the energy shock is broadening into consumer prices.

The Strait of Hormuz Effect

Five months after the U.S. began bombing Iran and Tehran retaliated by restricting passage through the Strait of Hormuz, the economic fallout is spreading well beyond gasoline pumps. Companies across the consumer, industrial and packaging sectors are telling investors they have raised prices or plan to do so, citing surging costs for raw materials, energy and freight.

Roughly 20% of the world's oil supply moved through the strait before the conflict, along with significant volumes of aluminium, fertilizer and other industrial commodities. The disruption has pushed benchmark U.S. crude futures to around $85 a barrel — up about 25% since the war began — while the national average for a gallon of regular unleaded gasoline has climbed to $4.11 from $2.98 at the start of the conflict.

Who's Raising Prices

Sherwin-Williams, the Cleveland-based paintmaker, announced an 8% price increase effective September 1 to offset rising oil-linked input costs. The company forecast raw material prices would rise further in the second half by high-single-digit percentages. Its shares surged more than 8% on Tuesday, their largest one-day gain in over four years.

"We were able to delay this increase for customers and avoid disrupting their business during the height of the paint-selling season."

— Heidi Petz, CEO, Sherwin-Williams

Illinois Tool Works shares shot up more than 10% after CFO Michael Larsen confirmed the company had raised prices during the spring quarter to more than offset costlier inputs, including resins used in automotive components and plastic six-pack rings.

Lamb Weston Holdings, the Idaho-based french-fry maker, raised North American prices to counteract rising transportation costs and surging edible-oil prices. "Demand for biodiesel has driven up the cost of most edible oils," CFO James D. Gray told investors.

Unilever, maker of Dove soap and Hellmann's mayonnaise, said pricing would "lead growth during the second half of the year," according to CFO Srinivas Phatak, as higher commodity costs flow through its supply chain.

Packaging Costs Squeeze Everyone

Packaging expenses have become a particular pressure point. Plastic bottles and bags are made from oil and natural-gas derivatives, while aluminium supplies have been reduced with a significant share of global production trapped behind the strait. All three of the largest U.S. box makers — International Paper, Smurfit Westrock and Packaging Corp. of America — announced price increases in rapid succession in July, citing rising costs for recycled materials and freight alongside tight supplies from recent containerboard mill closures that eliminated about 10% of U.S. production capacity.

Inflation Meets the Midterms

The price increases are cheered by investors — shares of manufacturers and consumer-staples companies have rallied — but economists warn of broader consequences. "Investors in these particular companies celebrate every price increase announcement, but of course collectively all of these price increase announcements are very bad for the economy," said Adam Josephson of Sakonnet Research.

The Fed voted 9-3 on Wednesday to leave interest rates unchanged, with Chairman Kevin Warsh acknowledging the challenge of assessing how the energy shock is broadening into the wider economy. Higher consumer prices threaten to complicate the interest-rate path and loom as a factor in this autumn's midterm elections.

What to Watch

The trajectory depends on whether the Strait of Hormuz reopens to normal tanker traffic. U.S.-Iran peace talks remain fragile, and companies warn the cost impact will persist even if a deal materializes. European Central Bank chief economist Philip Lane has said inflation is likely to remain above 3% for at least a year given "the long variable lag" of the war's economic effects.
